results.content: How do you convert an ER diagram to a relational schema? Converting an ER (Entity–Relationship) diagram to a relational schema is a systematic mapping that preserves entities, attributes, keys, and relationships while producing tables, keys, and constraints suitable for a relational database. Converting an ER (Entity–Relationship) diagram to a relational schema is a systematic mapping that preserves entities, attributes, keys, and relationships while producing tables, keys, and constraints suitable for a relational database. - Include the primary key attributes of the owner (identifying) entity as foreign key (FK) columns. - Table columns: owner entity’s PK (as FK) + attribute value (or values if composite). + Option B (if relationship has attributes or strong semantics): create a separate relation for the relationship; include both entity PKs as FKs and as composite PK (or add surrogate PK). + Add a FK column in the N-side entity table referencing the PK of the 1-side. + If the relationship has attributes, create a separate relation with both PKs (1-side PK as FK) and the relationship attributes; set PK = the N-side FK (or composite). + Create a join table (associative relation): include both entity PKs as FKs; composite PK = both PKs (or add surrogate PK). * Convert relationship attributes into the relationship table or into the appropriate entity table depending on cardinality and mapping choice. 1. I was asked to draw the ERD and relational diagram of a table, I previously assumed that the relational diagram was the same as a ERD so what is the difference? Commented Aug 31, 2014 at 6:15. Commented Aug 31, 2014 at 6:18. The "relational diagram" is probably supposed to show the physical columns and relations of such (as would be done in Access or another SQL designer) where the ERD just boxes the entities at a higher abstract level. ## 2 Answers 2. An **Entity Relationship Diagram** defines the relationship between entities and their attributes. In example, an ERD contains many-to-many relationships and do not include foreign keys. They are *implied.* In an ERD, we are simply visualising the entities, their attributes, and the relation between them. In a **Relational Model** we are referring to an implementation of our model. A relational model is basically a model of a possible database implementation. In short, an ERD is an abstract concept of our database, it speaks in entities and attributes, an entity model. A relational model defines formats and relations in a way a database could understand, a data model. > ERD is belongs to relationship between entities, it is different from relation model. **Relational Database:** A database that maintains a set of separate, related files (tables), but combines data elements from the files for queries and reports when required. **ERD:** A database model that describes the attributes of entities and relationship occurs between two or more entities. results.title: AiiDA 1.0, a scalable computational infrastructure for automated reproducible workflows and data provenance - PMC
results.content: Here, we introduce developments and capabilities required to reach sustained performance, with AiiDA supporting throughputs of tens of thousands processes/hour, while automatically preserving and storing the full data provenance in a relational database making it queryable and traversable, thus enabling high-performance data analytics. Like AiiDA, all of these are implemented and operated through the Python language, and provide new language constructs to design and automatically execute workflows (in parallel), and store the resulting data. Additionally, during execution AiiDA automatically stores all data and actions in the provenance graph (see “The Provenance Model”), including the workflows, the calculations and their inputs and outputs, to provide full traceability. For these reasons, AiiDA implements two additional processes: calculation jobs, to manage the execution of external codes through job schedulers, and work chains to implement and orchestrate long-running workflows with the possibility of pausing and restarting between steps. In order to allow the implementation of a performant tool, AiiDA uses a relational database to store the provenance graph with its links and nodes including most of their properties (see “Node properties”). To make the queries for ancestors and descendants at arbitrary distance as efficient as possible, early versions of AiiDA computed and stored the transitive closure (TC) of the graph (i.e., the list of all available paths between any pair of nodes) in a separate database table. To enable users to extend core functionalities to suit the needs of a specific discipline, AiiDA provides a flexible plugin system to add custom data types, to interface external simulation codes with specific input generators and parsers, to implement custom workflows, and more. AiiDA leverages the entry point system by defining several groups specific to the type of resources that a plugin can extend, for example aiida.data and aiida.workflows for new data types and workflows, respectively (ten groups are currently defined, to extend support to new codes, parsers, job schedulers, transport protocols to connect to remote computers, external databases, etc.). S.P.H. and M.U. designed the current provenance graph formalising the two provenance levels, incorporating the extension of B.K., and implemented it with contributions in both design and implementation by L.T., G.P., A.V.Y. and S.Z. B.K. developed an initial scheme for JSONB node attributes and their queries via the SQLAlchemy ORM.
